path.summary: Python is everywhere because it's easy to start and brutal to maintain at scale. This course gives you the mental models — names as stickers, mutable defaults as time bombs, the planner-vs-doer of types — that turn copy-paste survival into actual fluency. By the end you can read unfamiliar Python and write code that survives the next sprint.

audioChapters.label: Opening — why your variable bug isn't what you think

blocks.md:
Most Python bugs aren't logic bugs. They're *naming* bugs. You wrote `a = b` thinking you copied a thing; you actually pointed two stickers at the same thing. The two scenarios are visually identical and behaviorally divergent.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to read any line of Python and tell, instantly, whether it copies, aliases, or mutates. That's roughly 30 percent of all real-world Python bugs, gone.

blocks.caption: Names are stickers. They point at objects. They do not own them. When you assign one to another, you peel the sticker and slap it on the same object.

blocks.title: Mental model: stickers, not boxes
blocks.md:
Other languages teach you that variables are *boxes* you put values into. Python isn't that. **Python names are stickers** you peel off and stick onto objects.

This sounds like trivia. It's the difference between code that works in dev and code that mutates production data. We'll show you exactly how, in two moves.

blocks.caption: Watch a single list get aliased, mutated, and rebound in real time.

hi-IN.title: Tiffin-box wala analogy
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, Mummy ne ek tiffin pack kiya — `lunch`. Tu office mein bola "papa ke liye bhi same khaana lekar jaa raha hoon, isko `papa_lunch` bol". `papa_lunch = lunch`.

[long pause]

Dono ek hi tiffin hai. Tu lunch khaayega toh papa_lunch bhi khali. Yeh `=` ka kaam tiffin copy karna nahi tha. Bas dusra **sticker** chipka diya same tiffin pe.

en.title: The shared-tiffin moment
en.md: Mom packs one lunchbox. You label it `lunch`. Your colleague says "call mine `papa_lunch`" and you write `papa_lunch = lunch`. Now there's still one lunchbox with two labels. You eat from one, the other is also empty. Assignment didn't copy the lunchbox; it stuck a second label on the same one.

blocks.md:
When you write `a = [1, 2, 3]`, Python creates a list object somewhere in memory and points the name `a` at it. When you then write `b = a`, Python does **not** copy the list. It points another name `b` at the same object. `id(a) == id(b)` — true.

Now watch what happens depending on which operator you use next.

blocks.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a              # alias; same object
b.append(4)        # mutates the object both names point at
print(a)           # → [1, 2, 3, 4]   (surprise for newcomers)

b = b + [5]        # rebind — now b points at a NEW list [1,2,3,4,5]
print(a)           # → [1, 2, 3, 4]   (a unchanged)
print(b)           # → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
blocks.caption: The two operations look adjacent in code; one mutates, one rebinds. Read every line knowing which it is.

blocks.alt: Three states side by side. State 1: a and b both pointing at [1,2,3]. State 2: a and b both pointing at [1,2,3,4] (mutation). State 3: a still on [1,2,3,4], b moved to a new list [1,2,3,4,5] (rebind).

blocks.title: Translation moment: mutation vs rebinding, line by line

steps.label: Step 1 — Create the list, point a at it
steps.body: One list object lives in memory. One name a points at it.

steps.label: Step 2 — Alias
steps.body: No copy happens. b becomes a second sticker on the same paper bag.

steps.label: Step 3 — Mutate via b
steps.body: The single underlying list grows by one. Both names see the change because both point at the same object.

steps.label: Step 4 — Rebind b
steps.body: b + [5] creates a NEW list. The = points b at the new list. a is unchanged because nothing rebound a.
steps.code:
b = b + [5]
# a unchanged; b on a new list

steps.label: Step 5 — The diagnostic
steps.body: Look at the operator. = on the left of an assignment rebinds the name. Method calls or [] subscript-assignment mutate the object. They are visually similar; they do completely different things.

blocks.prompt:
After this code runs, what does `a` print?

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b = b + [4]
print(a)
```

choices.explain: Correct. `b = b + [4]` rebinds b to a new list. a was never touched after line 1.
Tempting if you remember move 1. But + creates a new list and rebinds b; it does NOT mutate the original. If the line had been `b.append(4)`, a would also be [1,2,3,4].
That would be `a = [4]`, a rebind on a's left side. We never wrote that.

choices.label: TypeError
choices.explain: Lists support concatenation with +; no error.

hi-IN.title: Bhai, paste karne se pehle ek question
hi-IN.md:
Stack Overflow se code paste kara. Test pass ho gaya. Prod mein deploy kara. Aadhi raat 2 baje pager bajne laga.

Deep mein dekha — ek `=` tha jaha `.copy()` hona chahiye tha. Pure 4 saal ki user history shared object pe likhi gayi. Migration script ne sabki email same kar di.

**Yaad rakh: Python ka `=` matlab "isi cheez ko ek aur naam de." Copy chahiye toh `list(x)` ya `dict(x)` ya `copy.deepcopy(x)` likh.**

en.title: The on-call moment
en.md: You paste code from Stack Overflow. Tests pass. You deploy. At 2 a.m. the pager goes off — every user's email is suddenly the same. The bug? One `=` where there should have been `.copy()`. Four years of user history written into a shared object. The fix is one line; the lesson is `=` aliases, it doesn't copy.

blocks.md:
Every Python developer trips on this exactly once. Then they tell the next one. Then we write courses about it.

Default values for function arguments are evaluated **once, at function definition time** — not every time the function is called. If you use a mutable default like `[]` or `{}`, all calls share the same default object. State leaks across calls in ways that look impossible.

blocks.code:
def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(add_item('apple'))   # → ['apple']
print(add_item('banana'))  # → ['apple', 'banana']  ← what?!
print(add_item('cherry'))  # → ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
blocks.caption: Three calls. Three different items. One basket that just keeps growing because the default `[]` was created once and reused forever.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing a function with a default argument basket=[]. An arrow shows the default list created once at function definition, sitting in memory. Three call arrows show all three calls reaching for the same shared list.
blocks.caption: The default `[]` is created at definition time. All calls share the one list. Mutate it once, you've mutated it for the next caller — and the next.

coach.name: PEP-8 Pranav
coach.role: Senior at standup who gently roasts your code

intro: I'm going to show you 5 Python patterns from real PRs. You tell me — *idiomatic*, *anti-pattern*, or *bug*?
No partial credit. The sleep deprivation is doing all the heavy lifting on these.

scenarios.situation:
```python
def append_log(msg, log=[]):
    log.append(msg)
    return log
```
scenarios.explain: Mutable default. The list persists across calls. Fix: `log=None` then `if log is None: log = []`.

scenarios.situation:
```python
items = [x*2 for x in range(5) if x%2==0]
```
scenarios.explain: List comprehension with filter; idiomatic. Reads as one sentence. The for-loop equivalent would take 4 lines for no gain.

scenarios.situation:
```python
result = []
for i in range(len(items)):
    result.append(items[i].upper())
```
scenarios.explain: Anti-pattern. Indexing into a list when you could iterate directly. Idiomatic: `result = [x.upper() for x in items]`.
The assert will fail at runtime. b is an alias of a. b[0] = 99 mutates the shared list. a is now [99,2,3].
Anti-pattern. Use `is not None` not `!= None`. Some objects override __eq__ in surprising ways; identity check is safer and is the PEP-8 idiom.

scenarios.situation:
```python
def chunk(items, size=100):
    return [items[i:i+size] for i in range(0, len(items), size)]
```
scenarios.explain: Default is an int (immutable), so no mutable-default problem. Comprehension is clean. Slice arithmetic is the conventional way.

blocks.title: The classic trap: mutable defaults
blocks.md:
Anytime a function signature has `def f(x=[]):` or `def f(x={}):` or `def f(x=set()):` — that's a bug waiting for production. The fix is the **None-sentinel pattern**:

```python
def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket
```

Memorize this shape. The `if basket is None` check is non-negotiable for any default that's a container.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps to safely refactor a function with a mutable default to use the None-sentinel pattern:

items.label: Identify the mutable default in the signature (any list, dict, or set literal)
items.detail: Scan the def line; flag any default that isn't a primitive.

items.label: Replace the default with None in the signature
items.detail: Now the default is immutable; cannot leak across calls.

items.label: Add a guard at the top: `if x is None: x = []`
items.detail: Restores the original behavior intent without the shared-state bug.

items.label: Run tests; if any test was relying on cross-call state, that's a bug too — fix the test
items.detail: Mutable-default 'features' are bugs even when intentional.

blocks.instruction: Refactor the buggy `add_item` so multiple calls do NOT share state. Use the None-sentinel pattern.
blocks.starter:
def add_item(item, basket=[]):
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

# Refactor below. The signature should still accept a `basket` arg.
blocks.expected:
def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

# Now each call without basket gets a fresh empty list:
print(add_item('apple'))   # ['apple']
print(add_item('banana'))  # ['banana']
# And explicit baskets still work:
print(add_item('cherry', basket=['date']))  # ['date', 'cherry']

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO statements that are TRUE about Python name semantics:

choices.label: `a = b` makes both names point at the same object
choices.explain: Correct. Assignment binds; it does not copy.

choices.label: `a += [1]` mutates if a is a list, but rebinds if a is a tuple
choices.explain: Correct, and counterintuitive. Lists support `__iadd__` (in-place add); tuples don't, so += falls back to `a = a + [1]`, which makes a NEW tuple-or-error.

choices.label: Default arguments are re-evaluated on every call
choices.explain: Inverse of the truth — they're evaluated once at definition time. This is the entire point of the mutable-default trap.

choices.label: `is` and `==` are interchangeable
choices.explain: Different operators. `is` checks identity (same object); `==` checks equality (same value). They diverge whenever you have aliases or proxy objects.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka "haan" vs Papa ka "haan"
hi-IN.md:
Indian household mein bhi yeh trap hai bhai.

Mummy se puchha *"chips kha sakta hoon?"* — jawab `True` hai. Roz puchhta hai, roz `True` aata hai. Tujhe lagta hai default response = haan.

Day 90: papa ke saamne pucha. Same default *expectation*. Aaj `False` aaya. Pura mood off ho gaya. **Default expectation tu fix kara tha at definition time. Reality har call par re-evaluate hoti hai.** PEP-8 nahi padha kya?

en.title: The 'parents-have-state' analogy
en.md: You ask one parent if you can do X. They say yes for the 50th time. You internalize "the answer is yes." You then ask the other parent assuming the same default. The reality re-evaluates per caller. Default expectations don't compose across callers — same bug, different domain.

blocks.title: Field Notes: One Equals Sign, 41,000 Wrong Settings
blocks.source: Anonymous backend engineer at PaisaPay (Bengaluru fintech, ~120 engineers)
blocks.story:
We shipped a 'remember last filter' feature on a Wednesday. By 02:14 a.m. Friday the on-call pager was on fire. A merchant in Indore had set his dashboard to show only failed UPI transactions. Within four hours, **41,287 other merchants** were also seeing only failed UPI transactions. Their actual filters were gone. Support inbox: 312 angry tickets, three of them in all caps in Marathi.

I bisected for ninety minutes before I saw it. The PR added a tiny helper:

```python
def get_user_prefs(user_id):
    prefs = DEFAULT_PREFS  # <-- the crime
    prefs['last_filter'] = load_filter(user_id)
    return prefs
```

`DEFAULT_PREFS` was a module-level dict. `prefs = DEFAULT_PREFS` did not copy it. It pointed a second sticker at the *same* dict. Every call mutated the global default. The first user to set a filter overwrote the default for every user the cache touched after them.

Fix was one line: `prefs = DEFAULT_PREFS.copy()`. Refund credits issued: ₹4.7 lakh. Post-mortem cost in engineering hours: roughly ₹11 lakh. Cost of the actual bug: zero, because `=` is free.

The junior who wrote it had two years of Java. In Java, `=` on a primitive copies. He assumed the same here. He wasn't wrong about Python; he was wrong about *which Python*.
blocks.takeaway: `=` aliases. It never copies. If you wrote `=` and meant 'give me my own version,' you wrote a bug — you just haven't paid for it yet.

blocks.title: Code Review at 11:47 p.m.
blocks.setup: It's Thursday night. The release train leaves at midnight. **Aakash**, the new grad on your team, just opened a PR titled *'add user notification preferences endpoint.'* Three files, 142 lines. He needs your LGTM in thirteen minutes or it slips a week. You open the diff. Veteran-CTO Vidya is pinged on the same review and is watching what you say.

coach.name: Veteran-CTO Vidya
coach.role: Two-time CTO, has seen this exact bug at three different companies

stages.prompt:
First file. The helper looks like this:

```python
def build_prefs(user_id, overrides={}):
    overrides['user_id'] = user_id
    overrides['updated_at'] = now()
    return overrides
```

Aakash says it works — he ran it locally, output looks fine. What do you flag?

options.label: Approve. The function returns a dict; the caller can ignore `overrides` if they don't pass one.
options.explain: This is the **mutable default trap**. `overrides={}` is evaluated **once** at definition time. Every call that omits `overrides` mutates the *same* dict. By call #2, it already has the previous user's `user_id` baked in. Vidya is grimacing.

options.label: Block. The default `overrides={}` is shared across calls. Use the `None`-sentinel pattern: `overrides=None` and `overrides = {} if overrides is None else overrides`.
options.explain: Exactly the textbook fix. The default expression is evaluated once at `def` time, so `{}` becomes a singleton. The sentinel pattern creates a fresh dict per call. This is the named trap from the lesson and Vidya nods.

options.label: Suggest a copy: `overrides = overrides.copy()` at the top of the function.
options.explain: Partial credit. It does protect the caller's dict from mutation, but the *shared default* is still the same dict every call — and `.copy()` on it still leaks the *previous* mutation if any caller mutated before `copy`. The sentinel is the canonical fix.

options.label: Approve with a TODO comment to revisit.
options.explain: TODO comments without an issue number are a CLAUDE.md violation, but more importantly: this is a **silent data-corruption bug**, not a style nit. It will only show up under load with the second concurrent request. You will not 'revisit.'

stages.prompt:
Second file. Aakash defends the next snippet — *'this is just shorthand, what's the issue?'*

```python
user_a = load_user(101)
user_b = user_a
user_b.preferences['theme'] = 'dark'
save(user_a)
save(user_b)
```

What's the actual behavior here?

options.label: Both `user_a` and `user_b` end up with `theme='dark'`, because `user_b = user_a` aliases — they're the same object. We just saved the same user twice.
options.explain: Correct. `=` peels the same sticker off and slaps it on `user_b`. There is one `User` object in memory. The `save(user_a)` and `save(user_b)` calls both write the same row. Worse: if there's an `updated_at` trigger, you've now logged two write events for one user.

options.label: `user_a` keeps its old theme; only `user_b` is dark, because Python passes by value.
options.explain: Python doesn't 'pass by value' the way Java does for primitives. `=` aliases. `user_a` and `user_b` point at the same dict. Both will show `dark`.

options.label: It's fine — Python's garbage collector handles the duplicate save.
options.explain: Garbage collection is about *unreachable* objects. This is reachable, mutated, and double-saved. GC has nothing to do with it.

options.label: It's mostly fine, but you should add `user_b = copy.deepcopy(user_a)` to be safe.
options.explain: Partial. `deepcopy` *would* break the alias, but only if the *intent* was to have two users. If the intent was one user, the right fix is to delete the second `save()`. Diagnose intent before you reach for `deepcopy`.

stages.prompt:
Third file. Aakash refactored the test helper:

```python
DEFAULT_NOTIFICATION_TYPES = ['email', 'sms', 'push']

def test_user(types=DEFAULT_NOTIFICATION_TYPES):
    types.append('whatsapp')
    return User(notif=types)
```

The test passes. He's confused why you keep making faces.

options.label: First call returns a user with 4 types. Second call returns 5. Third returns 6. The module-level list grows forever because every call appends to the *same* list.
options.explain: This is the mutable-default trap *plus* a module-level list aliased through the default. `DEFAULT_NOTIFICATION_TYPES` is now permanently corrupted for any other code that imports it. The test passes once. The next test in the suite gets `['email', 'sms', 'push', 'whatsapp', 'whatsapp']`.

options.label: Each call gets its own list, so the test is fine.
options.explain: No — `types=DEFAULT_NOTIFICATION_TYPES` does not copy the list. It binds the parameter `types` to the same list object. `.append` mutates it.

options.label: It's fine because lists are immutable in Python.
options.explain: Lists are mutable. Tuples are immutable. This is the most common mix-up and the one most likely to bite in a code review. Vidya is now drinking her chai a little faster.

options.label: It might be fine, but I'd write `types = types + ['whatsapp']` to be safe.
options.explain: Partial. `types + ['whatsapp']` creates a *new* list and rebinds `types` locally — the module-level list is no longer mutated. Good fix, but you also need to break the default-aliasing root cause: `types=None` with a sentinel.

stages.prompt: 11:54 p.m. Aakash pings: *'Bro, six minutes. Can you just approve and I'll fix in a follow-up?'* What do you do?

options.label: Block the PR. Post the three issues with one-line fixes for each. Offer to pair on the fix tomorrow morning. It's six minutes vs a 2 a.m. page next week.
options.explain: The grown-up answer. The three bugs in this PR are exactly the kind that pass code review, pass tests, and surface in production at 02:14 a.m. on a Friday. A one-week slip costs less than one Saturday on-call rotation, and Aakash learns the named traps with his name on them — the only way they actually stick.

options.label: Approve with comments. Trust him to fix them tomorrow.
options.explain: 'Fix in a follow-up' is the second-most expensive sentence in software, right after 'it works on my machine.' These are silent data-corruption bugs — the worst kind to defer because they don't crash; they just give wrong answers until someone notices.

options.label: Approve. He's a junior, the bugs are minor, and the release train is the priority.
options.explain: Mutable default + aliased global + cross-test contamination is not 'minor.' This is the exact shape of the PaisaPay incident — ₹4.7 lakh in refund credits, eleven lakh in eng hours. The release train is not the priority. Not waking up on Friday is.

options.label: Block, but instead of a comment, push your own fix to his branch.
options.explain: Partial. You unblock the train but you also rob Aakash of the lesson. He'll hit the same bug in a different shape next month. The whole point of the named traps is that *naming* them in review is what teaches them.

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. You blocked three silent data-corruption bugs in one review, named each trap from the lesson, and taught a junior the vocabulary at the same time. Vidya DMs you: *'send me your salary band, we're undershooting.'* This is what senior IC work actually looks like.
outcomes.good: Solid B+. You caught the bugs and stopped the release. You missed naming one of them precisely, but the PR didn't ship and the production data is safe. Aakash will learn — slower than ideal, but he'll learn. Go drink water.
outcomes.learn: C-tier — but the only way to get to S-tier is by losing this round once. Re-read the lesson on aliasing and the mutable-default trap. The next time you see `def fn(x=[])` or `b = a` followed by `b.append`, your hands should move toward the comment box before your brain finishes reading the line. Not your fault — every Python engineer pays this tuition once.

points: Python names are stickers, not boxes — `=` aliases, it does not copy
Mutation (`.append`, `[i] = `, `.update`) changes the object both names see
Rebinding (`x = ...` on the LHS) makes a name point at a new object
Default arguments are evaluated once at function definition; never use `[]` or `{}` as a default
The None-sentinel pattern (`if x is None: x = []`) is the canonical fix

lessons.subtitle: if, for, while — and the 'where the cat sat on' off-by-one

audioChapters.label: Mental model: the staircase, not the elevator

blocks.md:
Most non-Python languages teach you to think of control flow as a series of conditional jumps. Python prefers to think of it as a *conversation* — *for each item in this collection*, do this. *While this condition holds*, do that. The shape of the code matches the shape of the question.

By the end of this lesson, your loops will read like English, your if-chains will collapse, and you'll know exactly where the off-by-one bugs live.

blocks.title: Mental model: the staircase, not the elevator
blocks.md:
Other languages give you elevators — `goto`, exceptions for control flow, complex switch fall-through. Python gives you a staircase. **You climb one step at a time, and the structure of your code matches the structure of the data**.

When Python feels verbose, you're usually missing a more idiomatic shape. We'll show you the two shapes that replace 80 percent of imperative loops you've ever written.

blocks.caption: Watch a for-i loop and a for-each loop process the same list — count the lines, count the bugs.

hi-IN.title: Mumbai local — for-each ka real-world example
hi-IN.md:
Mumbai local mein har station pe ek hi sequence chalta hai: door khulta hai, log utarte hain, log chadte hain, door bandh hota hai, train chalti hai. Tu *for each station, do these 5 things* sochta hai — tu index nahi count karta.

Python ka `for x in items` matlab same hi hai. Tu loop counter nahi sambhalta — Python sambhalta hai. Tu sirf yeh batata hai *kya karna hai*. **Less ceremony, less off-by-one, less 2 baje raat ko debugging.**

en.title: The commute analogy
en.md: Every commuter knows: at each station, the same five things happen. You don't think 'station 1, station 2'; you think 'at each station, do this.' That's `for x in items`. Python handles the index; you just say what to do. Less ceremony, fewer off-by-ones, less 2 a.m. debugging.

blocks.md:
If you came from Java, C, or JavaScript-pre-2015, your fingers want to type `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)`. In Python, this is almost always wrong. Not stylistically — *mechanically* wrong. You introduce two variables (`i`, `items[i]`), an off-by-one risk, and three things you have to keep in sync.

Idiomatic Python: iterate over the items themselves. If you also need the index, use `enumerate`.

blocks.prompt: Which of these is the most idiomatic way to iterate `items` and print both index and value?

choices.label: `for i, x in enumerate(items): print(i, x)`
choices.explain: Correct. enumerate is the idiom; clean, no off-by-one risk.

choices.label: `for i in range(len(items)): print(i, items[i])`
choices.explain: Works but is anti-idiomatic. You're maintaining the index manually for no reason.

choices.label: `i = 0; while i < len(items): print(i, items[i]); i += 1`
choices.explain: Three lines where one would do, plus the off-by-one risk plus a manual increment. This is C, not Python.

choices.label: `[print(i, x) for i, x in enumerate(items)]`
choices.explain: Tempting because it uses enumerate, but list comprehensions for side effects are an anti-pattern — they build a throwaway list.

hi-IN.title: Off-by-one ka classic — chai-walla counting
hi-IN.md:
Tu chai-walla ko bola *"5 chai do."* Woh `range(5)` chala — 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. **Paanch chai mile.** Theek hai.

Lekin tu ne `range(1, 5)` likha hota — 1, 2, 3, 4 — sirf 4 chai milti. **The bug is in your boundary, not in your counting.**

Python ka `range(start, stop)` *stop ko exclude karta hai*. Ek baar yaad rakha, fir lagega kabhi galat nahi tha.

en.title: The boundary, not the count
en.md: Most off-by-one bugs aren't counting bugs; they're boundary bugs. Python's `range(start, stop)` excludes stop. Once that lives in your fingers, the bug class disappears.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The off-by-one trap (and how to never see it again)

blocks.md:
Off-by-one bugs come in two shapes:

1. **Boundary confusion**: did you mean `< n` or `<= n`? Python's `range(n)` gives you `0..n-1`. `range(1, n)` gives you `1..n-1`. The stop is exclusive; once that's muscle memory, half the off-by-ones vanish.
2. **Slice confusion**: `items[1:5]` gives 4 items (indices 1, 2, 3, 4). `items[:n]` is the first n. `items[-1]` is the last. The exclusive stop is the same rule everywhere.

The fix is not to be more careful. The fix is to *avoid manual indexing whenever possible*, which is the entire point of move 1.

blocks.prompt: Order these from most to least off-by-one prone (most prone first):

items.label: Manual `for i in range(len(items)): items[i]`
items.detail: Maximum surface area: range, len, indexing. Three places to slip.

items.label: `while i < len(items)` with manual increment
items.detail: Two surfaces: the bound and the increment. Easy to forget +=1.

items.label: `for i, x in enumerate(items)`
items.detail: Index is provided; no len() math, no manual increment. Hard to slip.

items.label: `for x in items`
items.detail: No index at all — there is no off-by-one to make.

blocks.instruction: Refactor this loop to be idiomatic. Two changes are needed: replace the for-i pattern, and remove the manual index management.

blocks.prompt: Which of the following are TRUE about Python iteration? (pick TWO)

choices.label: `range(5)` produces the integers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (stop is exclusive)
choices.explain: Correct. Memorize: stop is exclusive. Same rule for slicing.

choices.label: `enumerate(items)` yields `(index, item)` pairs and saves you a manual counter
choices.explain: Correct. enumerate is the idiomatic way to get index + item together.

choices.label: List comprehensions are slower than equivalent for-loops
choices.explain: False. Comprehensions are typically faster than equivalent for-loops in CPython because the loop runs in C; you're not dispatching method calls per iteration in Python.

choices.label: `zip` truncates to the shortest iterable silently — use `zip(strict=True)` or `itertools.zip_longest` if you need a different behavior
choices.explain: Tempting but this is an opinion-as-fact, not a definition. The first half is true (zip truncates silently); the second half is the recommended workaround. Whether that's a 'bug' or 'feature' is debated. As stated, the choice is too compound to land cleanly as 'true' — it tries to be both fact and prescription.

hi-IN.title: Hostel mess wala — counting items right
hi-IN.md:
Mess mein chapati count karta hai *"do, do, do, ek aur — yeh 7 hain"*. Tu sochta hai *"7 logon ke liye"*. Match.

Woh kabhi *"index 0 se 6 tak chapati"* nahi bolta. Kyun? Kyunki bewakoof nahi hai. Indexing tabhi useful hai jab tujhe index ki zaroorat ho. Warna, *for chapati in chapatis* — fast, simple, no off-by-one.

en.title: The mess-counter principle
en.md: The dining-hall server doesn't count 'index 0 to 6 chapatis.' They count chapatis. Use the iteration shape that matches the question. Indexes are a special case, not a default.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The 100% Discount That Slipped Through Range(len)
blocks.source: Anonymous senior engineer at ChamakDeals (Gurugram D2C marketplace, ~80M users)
blocks.date: October 2023, two days before Diwali sale
blocks.story:
Festive sale. Marketing wanted a *'one in a million'* gimmick — every millionth checkout, the user wins a 100% discount. PR went up Friday, demoed Saturday, deployed Monday morning at 09:00 IST.

By 10:42 a.m., the BI dashboard lit up. **One in a million** had become **roughly one in 999,999** — close enough that nobody flinched. Then 11:14: revenue was off plan by ₹3.2 lakh and climbing. By noon, ₹18 lakh.

The culprit was a perfect-looking loop:

```python
for i in range(len(checkouts)):
    if i % 1_000_000 == 0:
        checkouts[i].discount_pct = 100
```

Look closely. `range(len(checkouts))` starts at `0`. `0 % 1_000_000 == 0`. **The first checkout of every batch got 100% off.** Batches ran every 30 seconds. We were giving away one free order every 30 seconds during peak Diwali traffic.

The idiomatic version would have been `for i, c in enumerate(checkouts, start=1)`. The `start=1` is the entire fix. Total damage by the time the rollback completed at 12:47 p.m.: **₹47.3 lakh in unintended discounts**, 6,214 checkouts, one PM crying in the conference room, and a director-level post-mortem that produced exactly one rule: *no `range(len(...))` ships from this team again.*

The author was a five-year Python engineer. He'd written the same loop a thousand times. He just hadn't written it on a million-row collection on the day before Diwali.
blocks.takeaway: `range(len(x))` is a *boundary statement disguised as a count statement*. If your loop uses the index for anything other than indexing, you wanted `enumerate` — and you almost certainly wanted `start=1`.

blocks.title: Refactor Under the Senior's Gaze
blocks.setup: It's standup-plus-15. Veteran-CTO Vidya pulls up your screen on the big TV. *'Show me the discount-engine PR. We're doing it live.'* The team gathers. Your loop is sixty lines long. You have one hour and four pairs of eyes. **PM Sneha** is listening because the same engine ships her A/B tests next week.

coach.name: Veteran-CTO Vidya
coach.role: Reads code like she's reading a contract

stages.prompt:
First section of the loop:

```python
results = []
for i in range(len(orders)):
    if orders[i].status == 'paid':
        results.append(orders[i].amount)
```

Vidya: *'Rewrite this. Out loud. What's the most idiomatic Python form?'*

options.label: `results = [o.amount for o in orders if o.status == 'paid']`
options.explain: List comprehension. Reads as English: *'amounts of orders where status is paid.'* No index, no boundary, no off-by-one possible. This is the canonical translation of the 'collect things matching a condition' pattern.

options.label: `results = list(filter(lambda o: o.status == 'paid', orders))` then map.
options.explain: Functional but un-Pythonic. PEP 8 and Guido himself have said: prefer comprehensions over `filter`/`map` for readability. Also returns whole orders, not amounts — you'd need a second pass.

options.label: Keep the `range(len(...))` but rename `i` to `idx` for clarity.
options.explain: Renaming a code smell is not the same as removing it. The boundary trap from the lesson — and the Diwali story — lives inside `range(len(...))`. Better names don't fix off-by-one.

options.label: `for i, o in enumerate(orders): if o.status == 'paid': results.append(o.amount)`
options.explain: Better than `range(len)` because you don't double-index, but you're not using `i` for anything. If the index is unused, drop the `enumerate` and use a comprehension. Partial credit for instinct.

stages.prompt:
Next section. Same loop body now needs the *position* of each paid order (1-indexed, for a customer-facing receipt: *'order 1 of 3'*).

```python
for i in range(len(paid_orders)):
    paid_orders[i].position_label = f'Order {i} of {len(paid_orders)}'
```

What ships to the customer right now?

options.label: *'Order 0 of 3'*, *'Order 1 of 3'*, *'Order 2 of 3'*. The first customer sees 'Order 0', which looks broken. Fix: `enumerate(paid_orders, start=1)`.
options.explain: Bingo. The off-by-one trap, exactly as the Diwali field notes named it. `range(len)` and `enumerate` both default to 0-indexed. For human-facing labels, you almost always want `start=1`. Vidya nods.

options.label: *'Order 1 of 3'*, *'Order 2 of 3'*, *'Order 3 of 3'*. Looks fine.
options.explain: You skipped the trap. `range(len(x))` starts at 0. The first label will be *'Order 0 of 3'*. This will show up in a screenshot in the founder's WhatsApp by EOD.

options.label: It crashes at `len(paid_orders)` because you can't call `len` inside a loop.
options.explain: `len()` is fine inside a loop (just inefficient if recomputed). The bug is the indexing, not the call.

options.label: Replace `i` with `i + 1` in the f-string. Done.
options.explain: Functionally fixes the output, but you're patching the symptom. The named idiom is `enumerate(seq, start=1)`. Adding `+1` to indices is the smell that the lesson explicitly warned about — it's how the Diwali bug shipped.

options.label: Refactor to a `for` loop with a flag, or to two passes — one for refunds, one for non-refunds. Manual index increments in a `while` are off-by-one bait, especially when increments are conditional.
options.explain: Correct instinct. Manual `i +=` with conditional jumps is the most error-prone shape in Python control flow. Either separate the concerns into two passes, or pre-filter the refunds. The shape of the code should match the shape of the question.

options.label: Approve. It's a valid `while` loop, the bounds check is right.
options.explain: The bounds check is right *today*, on *this* data. The `i += 2` skips the next item — if that item is also a refund, you'll skip processing it. If the list ends on a refund, you'll do `i += 2` and your next iteration's `orders[i]` is past the end. The check catches it, but only because of `<`. One typo to `<=` and it's a crash.

options.label: Convert to `for i, o in enumerate(orders): ...` and keep the conditional skip.
options.explain: You can't skip iterations in a `for ... in enumerate` loop the way you can with manual `i +=`. Reassigning `i` inside the body has no effect on the next iteration. This would silently change behavior. Partial credit for the instinct toward `enumerate`, but the diagnosis is wrong.

options.label: Add a comment explaining the skip logic.
options.explain: Comments are not refactors. The next person — or you in three months — will still misread the skip and break it. Code should not need a comment to be safely modifiable.

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. You collapsed sixty lines into roughly fifteen, named the off-by-one trap by its full name, and pre-empted three bugs that would have shipped. Vidya: *'Send the diff to the team channel as a teaching example.'* PM Sneha smiles for the first time in this standup. You bought back forty minutes of your future on-call life.
outcomes.good: B+. The refactor is cleaner and shorter, the off-by-one is gone, and the loop reads like English. You missed one idiom (probably the comprehension or the `start=1`), but nothing that ships will harm a customer. Vidya gives you the *'fine, ship it'* nod.
outcomes.learn: C-tier — but every Python engineer trades one Diwali sale for this lesson. Re-read the boundary section. The next time you type `for i in range(len(...))`, treat it as a smell that the *real* loop you wanted is one of: `for x in seq`, `for i, x in enumerate(seq, start=1)`, or `[expr for x in seq if cond]`. Pick before you type.

points: Iterate over items, not indices — `for x in items`, not `for i in range(len(items))`
Use `enumerate(items)` when you need both index and item; never maintain `i` manually
`zip(a, b)` walks two collections in lockstep; cleaner than parallel indexing
Python ranges and slices are stop-exclusive — `range(5)` is 0..4, `items[:5]` is the first 5
Comprehensions are for collecting results; never use them for side effects

blocks.md:
Most beginner Python functions look like *imperative scripts wrapped in `def`*. They take 7 arguments, mutate global state, return None, and require ten test runs to figure out what they do.

This lesson teaches you to write functions that read like *plug-in tools*: clear inputs, one job, one return shape. The cost is small. The maintainability gain is enormous.

blocks.title: Mental model: the signature is a contract
blocks.md:
When you write `def get_user(user_id: int) -> User:`, you're signing a contract. *Give me an int. I'll give you a User. I won't reach outside this box for state. I won't surprise you.*

Most bad Python functions break the contract silently — they take 5 things, they read 3 globals, they sometimes return None, they sometimes raise. The contract is invisible because it was never written. **Type hints make it visible. Use them.**

blocks.caption: A function call animated as a stack frame opening and closing.

hi-IN.title: Bombay dabbawala — function ki signature ka real example
hi-IN.md:
Bombay dabbawala ka system 99.999% accurate hai. Kyun? Kyunki har dabba ke upar ek 6-character code hai — tiffin kahan se aaya, kahan jaayega, train kaunsi. **Yeh signature hai.** No ambiguity, no "kuch bhi de do, dekh lenge".

Tera function bhi same hona chahiye. Type hints daal — `(user_id: int) -> User`. Caller ko bhi clarity, future-tu ko bhi. Aaj 5 min lagenge, 6 mahine baad woh 5 min ka 5 ghante ka debugging session bachayenge.

en.title: The dabbawala signature
en.md: Mumbai's lunchbox-delivery system is 99.999% accurate because every box has a 6-character code — origin, destination, train. That's a signature. No ambiguity. Your function deserves the same. Type hints take five minutes to write and save five hours of debugging six months later.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Args, kwargs, and defaults that don't bite

blocks.md:
Python function signatures are flexible. Too flexible, if you don't know the rules:

- **Positional args** — required, in order: `def f(a, b)`
- **Keyword args with defaults** — optional, callable by name: `def f(a, b=10)`
- **`*args`** — capture extra positional args as a tuple. Use sparingly.
- **`**kwargs`** — capture extra keyword args as a dict. Use sparingly.

Rule of thumb: **prefer keyword args for anything beyond two parameters.** `f(user_id=42, send_email=True)` reads infinitely better than `f(42, True)`.

blocks.code:
# ❌ Hard to read at the call site
def notify(user, msg, urgent, retry, fallback): ...
notify(u, 'Login failed', True, False, True)  # what is True/False/True?

# ✅ Force keyword args after the first 2 with `*`
def notify(user, msg, *, urgent=False, retry=False, fallback=True): ...
notify(u, 'Login failed', urgent=True, fallback=True)  # readable

# ✅ Add type hints — your future self will thank you
def notify(
    user: User,
    msg: str,
    *,
    urgent: bool = False,
    retry: bool = False,
    fallback: bool = True,
) -> None: ...
blocks.caption: Use `*` in the signature to force keyword-only arguments for booleans and flags. Positional booleans are illegible at the call site.

coach.name: The Senior at Standup
coach.role: Has been doing this for a decade and is tired

intro: OK so I'm reviewing your PR. ☕
Here are 5 function signatures. Tell me — *good*, *fixable*, or *rewrite*.
Bonus points if you can articulate the bug in one sentence.

scenarios.situation:
```python
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b
```
scenarios.explain: Clean. Type-hinted, single responsibility, predictable return. This is the goal.

scenarios.situation:
```python
def process(data, opts=[]):
    opts.append('processed')
    return data
```
scenarios.explain: Mutable default + the function mutates a parameter that the caller might still hold a reference to + return value doesn't reflect what changed. Three bugs in three lines. Rewrite.

scenarios.situation:
```python
def send(user, msg, urgent, retry, log):
    ...
```
scenarios.explain: Five positional args, three of them booleans. Add `*` after the first two to force keyword-only for the flags. One-line fix; massive readability win at the call site.
SQL injection in a function called `get_user`. Type hints missing. Implicit None return on miss. This isn't a function; it's a vulnerability.
Will ZeroDivisionError on empty input. Add a guard: `if not values: return 0.0` (or raise, depending on contract). Otherwise the shape is fine.

A pass-through with no signature is a black box. The caller has no idea what to pass; the type checker can't help; the IDE can't autocomplete. *args/**kwargs is a tool, not a default — use only when you genuinely need variadic forwarding.

blocks.title: The classic trap: scope leak (UnboundLocalError)
blocks.md:
Inside a function, **assigning to a name** makes that name local for the entire function — even before the assignment line. So this looks innocent but blows up:

```python
count = 0

def increment():
    print(count)     # UnboundLocalError
    count = count + 1
```

Python sees `count = ...` later in the function and decides `count` is local. The `print(count)` then references a local that hasn't been bound yet.

Fixes (in order of preference): pass `count` as an argument, return the new value, or — only as last resort — `nonlocal` (in nested functions) or `global` (in modules). The `global` keyword is almost always a code smell.

blocks.prompt: Order these refactors of a 7-arg function from highest to lowest priority:

items.label: Add type hints to every parameter and the return
items.detail: Highest leverage. Makes the contract visible.

items.label: Convert the last 5 boolean params to keyword-only with `*`
items.detail: Massive call-site readability win; one-line change.

items.label: Replace any mutable defaults with the None-sentinel pattern
items.detail: Bug-prevention; non-negotiable for any list/dict default.

items.label: Split the function if it does more than one thing
items.detail: Architectural; do this last and only if the function is genuinely doing 2+ things.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO statements that are TRUE about Python function signatures:

choices.label: Adding `*` between positional and keyword args forces callers to use keywords for the keyword-only params
choices.explain: Correct. `def f(a, b, *, c, d)` — c and d are keyword-only.

choices.label: Type hints are checked at runtime by default
choices.explain: False. Hints are documentation by default; only tools like mypy / pyright check them. They are still hugely valuable — for IDEs, reviewers, and static analysis.

choices.label: `/` in a signature forces preceding params to be positional-only (Python 3.8+)
choices.explain: Correct. `def f(a, b, /, c)` — a and b are positional-only. Useful for library APIs where you don't want callers binding to the parameter names.

choices.label: Default arguments are re-evaluated on every call
choices.explain: Inverse of the truth. They are evaluated once at definition time. This is the entire mutable-default trap from lesson 1.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka function — strict signature
hi-IN.md:
Mummy ka *"khaane mein kya banao?"* function ki signature: `(option1: dish, option2: dish, mood: enum) -> dinner`.

Tu pucha *"kuch bhi de do."* — TypeError. "Kuch bhi" allowed nahi hai. Concrete option de.

Tu pucha *"sab khaa lunga."* — UnboundLocalError. *Sab* defined nahi hai is scope mein.

Mummy ne 35 saal mein yeh API design kara hai. Tera function bhi same strictness ka deserves.

en.title: Strictness is a feature
en.md: Strict function signatures feel pedantic at first. They feel like a rebate the second time someone calls your function and gets it right without asking you a single question. Be the parent, not the colleague who sighs.

blocks.title: Field Notes: UnboundLocalError on the Quarter-End Dashboard
blocks.source: Anonymous data engineer at LeharLogistics (Pune supply-chain SaaS, Series B)
blocks.story:
Quarter-end. Finance, Sales, and the founder were all refreshing the same Looker dashboard at 5 p.m. waiting for the *'Q3 close'* number. The pipeline that fed it had run every weekday for eleven months without incident.

At 17:03, the dashboard threw `UnboundLocalError: local variable 'total' referenced before assignment`. Not a crash on a remote server — a giant red toast in the browser, in front of the founder, on the day the Series C deck needed the number.

I bisected. The diff was forty minutes old:

```python
total = 0

def compute_revenue(orders):
    if len(orders) == 0:
        return 0
    for o in orders:
        total = total + o.amount  # <-- crime
    return total
```

The author had added `total = total + o.amount` inside the function, intending to use the module-level `total`. Python saw an assignment to `total` *anywhere* in the function, decided `total` was a **local** variable for the *whole* function, and so the read on the right-hand side referenced the not-yet-assigned local. The module-level `total` might as well not exist.

The original code had been `total += o.amount` after a `total = 0` *inside* the function. Someone had refactored, hoisted `total = 0` out for *'reusability,'* and triggered the trap. Eleven months of green builds; one quarter-end at 17:03.

Fix took eight seconds: move `total = 0` back inside the function. Investor call was delayed by twenty minutes. The founder learned what `UnboundLocalError` means. He has not forgotten.
blocks.takeaway: Python decides scope by *static analysis of assignments*, not by what runs first. One `=` anywhere in a function makes the name local for the *entire* function — and the read above it will fail with `UnboundLocalError`.

blocks.title: Designing the Notification Function
blocks.setup: **PM Sneha** wants a *'send notification'* function. Simple: takes a user, sends a message. Two days into the spec, it has eight new flags. Veteran-CTO Vidya is in the design-review thread asking pointed questions. You hold the pen on the signature.

coach.name: Veteran-CTO Vidya
coach.role: Will absolutely send your PR back if the signature looks like a Christmas tree

stages.prompt:
Sneha's first ask: *'Send a notification to a user via email or SMS, with optional WhatsApp, optional in-app banner, with a delay, with a priority, with a category, and the ability to skip if the user has DND on.'*

First-draft signature?

options.label: `def send_notification(user, message, email=True, sms=False, whatsapp=False, in_app=False, delay_sec=0, priority='normal', category='general', skip_if_dnd=True):`
options.explain: This is the *'Christmas tree signature'* the lesson warned about. Nine arguments, mixed positional and keyword, no clear contract. Six months from now, every call site is `send_notification(u, m, True, False, True, False, 0, 'normal', 'billing', True)` and nobody can tell which boolean is which. Vidya is sharpening her review pen.

options.label: `def send_notification(user, message, *, channels: list[str], delay_sec: int = 0, priority: Priority = Priority.NORMAL, category: Category = Category.GENERAL, respect_dnd: bool = True) -> NotificationResult:`
options.explain: Keyword-only after `*`, so call sites are self-documenting. `channels` is a list (open-set, not 4 booleans). Enums for the closed-set categoricals. Type hints. Return type. This is the contract version. Vidya nods.

options.label: `def send_notification(user, message, **opts):` and let callers pass whatever.
options.explain: Hides the contract entirely. The reader of `send_notification` has no idea what `opts` accepts. The lesson named this anti-pattern: `**kwargs` is for *genuine* variadic forwarding, not for laziness about defining a signature.

options.label: `def send_notification(user, message, channels=['email'], delay_sec=0, priority='normal', category='general'):`
options.explain: Hits the **mutable default trap** from lesson 1 — `channels=['email']` is the same list across calls, and any `.append` will leak. Also no keyword-only, no return type, no enums. Partial credit for trying to consolidate channels into a list.

stages.prompt: Sneha pings: *'Wait, also — can it sometimes be scheduled for a specific datetime instead of a delay? And can it batch with other notifications to the same user?'*

options.label: Add `send_at: datetime | None = None` and `batch_with: list[NotificationId] | None = None` to the same signature.
options.explain: You're starting to grow the Christmas tree back. `delay_sec` *or* `send_at`, but not both, is a state machine smuggled into a parameter list. Same with batching. The signature should not encode mutually exclusive modes.

options.label: Split into two: `send_notification(...)` for immediate/delayed and `schedule_notification(send_at, ...)` for absolute-time. Batching becomes its own function: `batch_notifications(notifications: list[NotificationDraft])`.
options.explain: Excellent. *One function, one job.* When mutually exclusive modes show up, that's the universe telling you it's two functions. Batching is a different operation entirely — it takes drafts, not single sends. Vidya: *'Yes.'*

options.label: Add a `mode: Literal['delay', 'absolute', 'batch']` arg and validate inside.
options.explain: Better than option (a) but you've moved the state machine from the type system into a runtime check. Now your function body is a giant `if mode == ...` and the caller has to read your function to know which other args are valid in which mode.

options.label: Refuse the change. Tell Sneha the spec is too big.
options.explain: Refusing scope changes is a PM-relationship-destroying move. The right answer is *'yes, and here's the cleaner shape.'* Disagreeing on the shape is fine; refusing the work is not.

stages.prompt: Sneha approves the split. Now Vidya: *'Show me how the function returns. Success vs failure vs partial — what does the caller get?'*

options.label: `-> bool` — `True` if sent, `False` if not.
options.explain: Throws away every useful piece of information. *Why* did it fail? Which channel? Was it a retryable failure or a permanent one? `bool` returns are the *'we'll figure it out from the logs'* anti-pattern.

options.label: `-> NotificationResult` where `NotificationResult` is a typed result with `status: Literal['sent', 'partial', 'failed']`, `delivered_channels: list[str]`, `failed_channels: list[ChannelFailure]`, and `retryable: bool`.
options.explain: This is the *Result-shape* return. The caller can branch on `status`, log the failures, and decide whether to retry. Aligns with the project's `Result<T,E>` rule from CLAUDE.md and the lesson's *'one return shape'* principle.

options.label: `-> None` and raise an exception on failure.
options.explain: Mixes the success path with the framework boundary. Exceptions for *exceptional* states; partial-failure of a multi-channel send is a *normal* state. The lesson and CLAUDE.md both say: return Result, don't throw.

options.label: `-> dict` — flexible, callers can read whatever keys they need.
options.explain: Untyped dicts are signature death. Six months from now, nobody knows which keys are guaranteed. This is the *'stringly typed'* anti-pattern in dict form.

stages.prompt: Final stage. Sneha: *'One last thing — for the in-app channel, the function needs to write to the in-app feed table. Should that be inside `send_notification`?'*

options.label: Yes. Inline the write. One function, one call, simpler for callers.
options.explain: *'One function does everything'* is the opposite of *'one job.'* Now `send_notification` is a notification dispatcher *and* a database writer *and* a transaction manager. It's also un-testable without a real DB.

options.label: No. `send_notification` calls `in_app_channel.deliver(user, message)`, and `InAppChannel` is a separate class with the DB write. The notification function knows nothing about the storage layer.
options.explain: Single responsibility. Each channel is a strategy. `send_notification` orchestrates; channels execute. Testable with a fake `InAppChannel`. Vidya: *'This is the function I would approve in five minutes.'*

options.label: Yes, but only if the DB write is inside a `try/except` that swallows failures.
options.explain: Swallowed exceptions are how data corruption ships silently. Worse, you've coupled the function to the DB *and* hidden the failure. Two anti-patterns for the price of one.

options.label: Inline the write but put it behind a feature flag for emergency removal.
options.explain: Feature flags are for behavior changes, not for compensating for bad architecture. Partial credit for caring about reversibility, but the right reversibility is *'replace one channel implementation,'* not *'flip a flag in production.'*

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. You held the line on the signature, split the function when the spec asked for two modes, returned a typed Result, and isolated the storage layer behind a channel abstraction. Vidya forwards the design doc to the eng-all channel: *'this is the standard.'* Sneha gets her feature, you get your weekend, and nobody gets paged at quarter-end.
outcomes.good: B-tier. The signature is cleaner than the first draft, you caught the mutable-default trap and the Christmas tree, and the function is roughly testable. Vidya leaves three review comments and signs off. The next iteration will get the rest.
outcomes.learn: C-tier — but the design instincts are learnable in a way the bugs aren't. Re-read the function-design lesson. The two questions to ask of every signature: (1) *can the caller read this without opening my code?* and (2) *is there exactly one job here, or did two jobs sneak in?* If either answer is no, refactor before you ship.

points: A function signature is a contract — make it visible with type hints
Force keyword-only args (with `*`) for booleans and flags; positional booleans are illegible
Mutable defaults are bugs; use the None-sentinel pattern
Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local for the whole function — pass values in, don't reach for globals
`*args, **kwargs` is a tool, not a default — never use it just to avoid declaring a real signature

blocks.md:
Most Python performance bugs you'll meet in your first year aren't algorithmic. They're container choice. Someone reached for a `list` when they wanted a `set`, or a `dict` when they wanted a `Counter`, and turned an O(n) operation into O(n²).

By the end of this lesson, you'll pick a container in three seconds based on how you plan to access the data. The 'right answer' is almost always obvious once you ask the right question.

Each container exists because it answers a different question fast.

- *In what order did these arrive?* → **list**
- *Have I seen this one before?* → **set**
- *What's the value for key X?* → **dict**
- *I want a fixed bundle that I can use as a dict key* → **tuple**

The shape isn't an aesthetic choice. It's the difference between O(1) and O(n).

hi-IN.title: Sabzi-mandi pe sab containers ek saath
hi-IN.md:
Sabzi-mandi mein khada ho. Vendor ke paas:

- **Tokri (list)** — pyaaz, 5 kg, ek ke peeche ek
- **Khaate ka register (dict)** — `'Sharma uncle': 240, 'Patel aunty': 150`
- **Color-coded sticker (set)** — red sticker = paid, blue = pending. Same sticker do baar nahi lagta
- **Sealed packet (tuple)** — `(item, weight, price)` — change nahi ho sakta, identity de sakta hai

Tu list mein lookup karega "Sharma uncle ka kitna baki?" — pura register page-by-page padhega. **Galat container chuna toh O(n) ka tax bharega har query pe.**

en.title: Containers everywhere, all at once
en.md: Walk through any market and you see all four containers in physical form: a basket of onions (list), a ledger by name (dict), color-coded paid/unpaid stickers (set), and sealed packets you don't open (tuple). Each one answers a different question fast. Pick wrong and you pay the linear-search tax forever.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Pick by access pattern, not by data type

blocks.md:
Three diagnostic questions, in order:

1. **Do I need uniqueness?** → set
2. **Do I need to look up by key?** → dict
3. **Do I need order, with duplicates?** → list

If you find yourself writing `if x not in items: items.append(x)` over a list, you wanted a set. If you're writing `for u in users: if u.id == target: ...`, you wanted a dict keyed by id. The wrong choice is fine for 100 items and unbearable for 100,000.

blocks.caption: Same goal, two containers, two complexity classes. Read the access pattern; pick the container.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'count how many distinct customers ordered each product'

steps.label: 1. English
steps.body: For each product, count how many distinct customers ordered it.

steps.label: 2. Pick the outer container
steps.body: We need a count *per product*, looked up by product. That's a dict keyed by product.
steps.code:
from collections import defaultdict
counts = defaultdict(set)

steps.label: 3. Pick the inner container
steps.body: Distinct customers — uniqueness — is a set. defaultdict(set) auto-creates an empty set the first time we touch a key.

steps.label: 4. Compress to the answer
steps.body: Convert each set to its size for the final report.
steps.code: report = {p: len(custs) for p, custs in counts.items()}

steps.label: 5. The diagnostic
steps.body: Why this shape? Outer dict because we look up by product. Inner set because we deduplicate customers. The shape of the data structure mirrors the shape of the question.

blocks.prompt: You need to check membership against a 100,000-item collection 1,000 times. Which container is correct?

choices.label: set — O(1) lookup, total ~1,000 ops
choices.explain: Correct. Hash-based membership in O(1).

choices.label: list — O(n) lookup, total ~100,000,000 ops
choices.explain: Functionally works; will burn 100 million comparisons. This is the bug class beginners write into production weekly.

choices.label: tuple — same as set but immutable
choices.explain: Tuples have O(n) membership lookup, just like lists. Immutability and hash-based lookup are different properties.

choices.label: dict — but only if you don't care about the values
choices.explain: Tempting because dicts are O(1) lookup; but a set is the correct shape when you only care about membership. A dict with garbage values is a code smell.

hi-IN.title: Aadhaar card test — dict key kaisi honi chahiye
hi-IN.md:
Aadhaar number ek 12-digit fixed string hai. Tu use kabhi alag *banaata* nahi — bas use karta hai. Yeh **immutable** hai. Yahi reason hai ki Aadhaar number good database key banta hai.

Python mein same rule: **dict key immutable honi chahiye** — string, int, tuple. List nahi, dict nahi, set nahi. Mutable cheez ko key banaya toh hash badal sakta hai mid-flight, aur Python tujhe `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'` thappad maar dega.

en.title: Identity numbers and dict keys
en.md: Stable identifiers (passport number, Aadhaar, email) make good dict keys because they don't change. Lists, dicts, and sets cannot be dict keys precisely because they can change. Python won't let you try; that's the `unhashable type` error.

blocks.text: Move 2 — Comprehensions and the unhashable-key trap

blocks.md:
Comprehensions are the idiomatic way to build all four containers from another iterable. Same shape, different brackets:

```python
[x*2 for x in items]                   # list comprehension
{x*2 for x in items}                   # set comprehension
{x: x*2 for x in items}                # dict comprehension
(x*2 for x in items)                   # generator expression (lazy)
```

**The trap**: dict keys must be hashable, which means immutable. Try to use a list or dict as a key and you get `TypeError: unhashable type`. Use a tuple instead — tuples of immutable elements are hashable.

blocks.title: The classic trap: list as a dict key
blocks.md:
Anytime you reach for `d = {[1,2]: 'a'}` or `d[some_list] = ...`, Python raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`. The fix is almost always to convert the key to a `tuple`:

```python
d = {(1, 2): 'a'}     # works
d[tuple([1, 2])] = 'b'  # works
```

If you genuinely need a key that's a *set* of values (order doesn't matter), use `frozenset`:

```python
d[frozenset({'sql', 'python'})] = 'data engineer'
```

blocks.prompt: Order these from most idiomatic to least, for: 'collect distinct domains from a list of email addresses':

items.label: `{e.split('@')[1] for e in emails}` — set comprehension
items.detail: One line, exactly the right container.

items.label: `set(e.split('@')[1] for e in emails)` — set from generator
items.detail: Two-character difference; same result. Mildly less idiomatic but fine.

items.label: Build a list of all domains, then `set(...)` it
items.detail: Allocates a throwaway list. Works; wastes memory.

items.label: Manual `seen = []; for e in emails: ...if not in...append`
items.detail: O(n²); the bug from earlier in this lesson.

blocks.instruction: Refactor this O(n²) deduplication into idiomatic Python. Bonus: also produce a `dict` of domain → count of users.
blocks.starter:
emails = ['a@x.com', 'b@y.com', 'c@x.com', 'd@z.com', 'e@y.com']

domains = []
for e in emails:
    d = e.split('@')[1]
    if d not in domains:
        domains.append(d)

print(domains)

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO statements that are TRUE about Python containers:

choices.label: `set` and `dict` provide O(1) average-case membership lookup; `list` and `tuple` are O(n)
choices.explain: Correct. Hash tables vs. linear scan. This is why container choice is a complexity decision.

choices.label: Tuples can be used as dict keys; lists cannot
choices.explain: Correct. Tuples are immutable (and so are their hashes — assuming all elements are hashable). Lists are mutable, so unhashable, so cannot be keys.

choices.label: List comprehensions always run faster than the equivalent for-loop
choices.explain: Usually faster, not always. For pure side-effect loops (no result collected), a comprehension wastes memory building a list you discard. Use a comprehension when you want the result; a for-loop when you only want side effects.

choices.label: Dict comprehensions work but set comprehensions don't exist
choices.explain: Both exist. `{x for x in items}` is a set comprehension; `{k: v for k, v in pairs}` is a dict comprehension. The braces vs colon tells Python which.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka container choice
hi-IN.md:
Mummy kabhi tomatoes shopping bag mein nahi rakhti — fridge ke specific drawer mein. Daal mein achaar nahi mix hota — alag jar. Pickles mein dates ki list nahi — ek single tuple `(date, type)` har piece pe.

Mummy ka containerization 40 saal pe perfect hai. Tu ne ek sprint mein perfect karna hai. Same diagnostic — *kya question hai, woh shape kya hai*.

en.title: Containerization at home
en.md: Every Indian (and most non-Indian) kitchens run on disciplined container choice. Tomatoes don't go in the rice container; pickles don't go in the dry-snack jar. Each container exists because it answers a different question quickly. Programs work the same way.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Nightly Job That Grew From 3 Minutes to 4 Hours
blocks.source: Anonymous platform engineer at SaharaMart (Hyderabad grocery delivery, 14M MAU)
blocks.story:
Our nightly fraud-flagging job had a service-level objective: finish before 04:30 IST so the morning ops team could review flagged orders over chai. For sixteen months it ran in roughly **2 minutes 50 seconds**. Then, over four weeks, it crept up: 4 minutes, 12, 47, 88, **4 hours 11 minutes**. The 06:30 standup got an awkward *'…the report isn't ready yet'* every morning.

The SRE on rotation blamed the database. The DBA blamed the network. I blamed nobody and read the code:

```python
seen_order_ids = []
for order in todays_orders:
    if order.id not in seen_order_ids:
        seen_order_ids.append(order.id)
        process(order)
```

`order.id not in seen_order_ids` on a **list** is O(n). Inside a `for` loop over the same orders, that's **O(n²)**. When `todays_orders` was 30,000 rows (sixteen months ago), n² was 900M comparisons — fast on modern hardware. After Diwali expansion to Tier-2 cities, `todays_orders` was **180,000** rows. n² became **32.4 billion** comparisons. The database was innocent.

Fix: `seen_order_ids = set()`. `in` on a set is O(1). Job time the next night: **2 minutes 11 seconds**. The PR was three characters: `[]` to `set()` and `.append` to `.add`. The code review took longer than the change.

The cost wasn't compute. The cost was four weeks of *'the report isn't ready'* eroding ops trust, and one all-hands where an exec said *'Python doesn't scale'* — a sentence that haunts me.
blocks.takeaway: The wrong container is almost never an algorithm problem; it's a *shape* problem. *'Have I seen this?'* wants a `set`. *'How many?'* wants a `Counter`. *'Look up by key?'* wants a `dict`. List is the default — and almost never the right answer past 10K rows.

blocks.title: Refactor Before Tomorrow's Batch
blocks.setup: It's Monday, 7:42 p.m. Tomorrow's batch run kicks off at 02:00. **Aakash** pings you: *'bro, the dedup pipeline ran for 9 hours yesterday — it has to finish in under 2 hours tomorrow or finance will lose their mind. Veteran-CTO Vidya CC'd. Help?'* You open the file. It's worse than you feared.

coach.name: Veteran-CTO Vidya
coach.role: Will quietly walk past your desk if the fix isn't shipped by 9 p.m.

options.label: Use a `set` for the seen-IDs and keep the order: `seen = set(); unique = []; for o in orders: if o.id not in seen: seen.add(o.id); unique.append(o)`. O(n).
options.explain: Textbook. `set` membership is O(1) average. You preserve original order with the `unique` list and use the set only for the membership question. This is the canonical *'dedup while preserving order'* idiom.

options.label: `return list(set(orders))` — one line.
options.explain: Two problems: (1) `Order` objects need to be hashable, which usually requires implementing `__hash__` and `__eq__`. (2) `set()` does not preserve insertion order. If downstream code assumes order, you've silently broken it.

options.label: Sort `orders` by `id`, then dedup adjacent. O(n log n).
options.explain: Better than O(n²) but worse than the set approach, *and* you've changed the order. Reaching for sort when you wanted membership is the wrong-shape choice from the lesson.

options.label: Add `@lru_cache` to the function and rerun.
options.explain: `lru_cache` caches *function calls by argument tuple*. It does nothing inside this function body. Also, `orders` is a list — not hashable — so `lru_cache` would crash on the first call.

options.label: `from collections import Counter; return Counter(o.customer_id for o in orders)`
options.explain: `Counter` is the named container for *'how many of each.'* One line, faster than the dict version, returns a dict-like that supports `.most_common()`, addition, subtraction. The lesson's *'shape matches the question'* in its purest form.

options.label: `counts = defaultdict(int); for o in orders: counts[o.customer_id] += 1; return counts`
options.explain: Better than the original — no `if-in-else` — and uses `defaultdict` correctly. But `Counter` exists for exactly this case and is even more idiomatic. Partial credit for picking the right family of container.

options.label: `return {o.customer_id: orders.count(o.customer_id) for o in orders}`
options.explain: Disaster. `orders.count(...)` is O(n) and you call it once per row — back to O(n²). Also computes the count multiple times for the same customer. The exact bug class from the field notes, in dict-comprehension clothing.

options.label: Use `pandas.value_counts` after converting to a DataFrame.
options.explain: If you're already in pandas, sure — but loading pandas just for this is a 200ms import for an O(n) operation. Tool-fit failure. Stay in stdlib for stdlib-shaped problems.

options.label: Lists can't be dict keys because they're mutable. Use a tuple: `key = (order.region, order.payment_method)`. Tuples of immutable values are hashable.
options.explain: Exactly the named trap from the lesson. Hashable requires immutable (so the hash never changes after insertion). Tuples of strings are immutable; lists are not. Vidya nods from her desk.

options.label: Use `str(key)` to convert the list to a string and use that as the key.
options.explain: Works but is a code smell. You've stringified structured data; now everything that reads `buckets` has to parse the key back. Also `str(['a', 'b'])` and `str(['a', 'b '])` (trailing space) hash to different keys silently.

options.label: Use `frozenset(key)` instead.
options.explain: `frozenset` *is* hashable, but it loses order — `frozenset(['UPI', 'south'])` equals `frozenset(['south', 'UPI'])`. If region and payment-method should be a *positional* key, that's wrong. Tuple is the right shape.

options.label: Switch `buckets` to a `defaultdict(list)` and use `tuple(key)`. Drops the `if/else` and fixes the key.
options.explain: Actually quite good — `defaultdict(list)` *plus* tuple key is the cleaner version of the whole block. Marking partial because the question asked specifically about the key crash, but this is a stronger refactor end-to-end.

stages.prompt: 8:47 p.m. The dedup, counter, and bucketing are fixed. Aakash: *'should we add a cache?'* What's your call?

options.label: No. Measure first. The original 9-hour run was an O(n²) bug, not a missing cache. With the set + Counter fixes, run it once and time it. Add caching only if there's still a hot path.
options.explain: *Measure before you optimize* and *the wrong container masquerades as a slow algorithm*. You've already removed two O(n²)s — the most likely outcome is the job is now fast enough. Adding a cache before measuring just adds invalidation bugs.

options.label: Yes. Cache aggressively. Caches always make things faster.
options.explain: *Two hard problems in CS: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors.* The job runs once a night. Caches are for repeated reads; one-shot batch jobs rarely benefit and almost always pay an invalidation cost.

options.label: Add `@lru_cache` to every function that returns a value.
options.explain: `lru_cache` works on hashable args and pure functions. A pipeline that processes 240K rows once doesn't have repeated calls to cache. You'd add overhead, not save time.

options.label: Cache the dedup result on disk so tomorrow's run can reuse it.
options.explain: *Tomorrow's orders are different orders.* Disk-caching the dedup of *yesterday's* data doesn't speed up *tomorrow's* run. Partial credit if the intent was to cache lookup tables (regions, payment methods) — but that's not what was asked.

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. You took a 9-hour pipeline to under 2 hours by changing four characters in three places. Vidya walks past, sees the diff, says: *'good. Go home.'* Aakash buys you a samosa the next morning. The 06:30 standup is short for the first time in five weeks.
outcomes.good: B+. The set fix and the Counter fix shipped. The bucketing got cleaner. The pipeline runs in 12 minutes instead of 9 hours. Vidya is happy, Aakash is grateful, and you only worked an hour past 9 p.m.
outcomes.learn: C-tier — but container-choice intuition is the difference between *'Python is slow'* and *'I picked the wrong shape.'* Re-read the lesson. The three-second decision: *'how will I access this?'* If the answer is *'check membership,'* it's a set. *'Count things,'* it's a Counter. *'Look up by key,'* it's a dict. List is the default and almost always wrong past 10K rows.

points: Pick a container by access pattern, not by data type — uniqueness → set, lookup-by-key → dict, ordered-with-dups → list
`set` and `dict` membership is O(1); `list` and `tuple` are O(n). Wrong container = silent quadratic blow-up
Comprehensions exist for all four shapes — `[]`, `{}` (dict), `{...}` (set), `()` (generator)
Dict keys must be immutable — strings, ints, tuples, frozensets. Use `tuple()` when you need to key on what looks like a list
Reach for `Counter`, `defaultdict`, and `frozenset` from `collections` before reinventing them

hi-IN.title: Indian accountant ka pipeline
hi-IN.md:
Indian CA ka kaam — exact same pipeline:

1. Bills aatey hain (CSV) — handwritten, photocopied, kuch mein date 12/3/24, kuch mein 12-3-2024
2. Transform — har bill ko proper format mein convert
3. Summarize — ledger total, GST split
4. Output — clean JSON-style return file Income Tax department ke liye

CA bhi 80% time bills ka format normalize karne mein lagata hai. Logic 20% hai. **Programming bhi same hai.** Boundaries pe sab kuch verify kar.

en.title: Same pipeline, different domain
en.md: An accountant's workflow is the same four stages: receive (messy bills), transform (normalize dates, line-items), summarize (totals, splits), write (clean return). They spend 80% of their time on boundaries too. Same pipeline, different runtime.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Read and validate at the boundary

blocks.md:
Real CSVs are not the CSVs in tutorials. They have:

- Inconsistent date formats (`2024-03-12`, `12/03/2024`, `Mar 12 2024`)
- Empty cells where you expected numbers
- Trailing whitespace in keys (`'name '` vs `'name'`)
- Encoding issues (a stray `\ufeff` BOM at the start of the first column name)
- Rows that are 8 columns when you expected 7

Don't try to handle all of this gracefully in the middle of your pipeline. **Validate up front, fail loudly, fix the input.** The clean middle is what makes debugging tractable.

blocks.code:
import csv
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Iterator

def read_orders(path: str) -> Iterator[dict]:
    with open(path, encoding='utf-8-sig') as f:    # -sig handles BOM
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for i, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):  # row 1 is header
            try:
                yield {
                    'order_id': int(row['order_id'].strip()),
                    'customer': row['customer'].strip(),
                    'amount': float(row['amount']),
                    'date': datetime.strptime(row['date'], '%Y-%m-%d').date(),
                }
            except (KeyError, ValueError) as e:
                # Fail loudly, but with the row number
                raise ValueError(f'Row {i} malformed: {row}; reason: {e}') from e
blocks.caption: Generator + DictReader + utf-8-sig + per-row validation with line number. This is the boundary discipline.

blocks.prompt: Reading a CSV with `open(path, encoding='utf-8-sig')` instead of `'utf-8'` does what?

choices.label: Strips a leading byte-order mark (BOM) from the first column name if present
choices.explain: Correct. UTF-8 files exported from Excel often carry a 3-byte BOM at the start; `utf-8-sig` skips it. Without this, your first column name becomes `'\ufeffname'` and every lookup against `'name'` fails.

choices.label: Signs the file with a checksum
choices.explain: Did not read carefully. The `-sig` is for the byte-order-mark signature, not a cryptographic signature.

choices.label: Treats the file as little-endian UTF-8
choices.explain: Endianness applies to UTF-16, not UTF-8. UTF-8 is byte-orderless.

choices.label: Disables decoding entirely
choices.explain: Inverse of what -sig does — it's still UTF-8 decoded; just BOM-aware.

coach.name: Pickle Aunty
coach.role: Reads tracebacks faster than a Vipassana monk reads minds

intro: Main har stack se batauungi — *boundary bug, middle-logic bug, ya environment bug*?
And then I'll tell you the FIRST line you should read in each. Not the last. The first.

scenarios.situation: `ValueError: could not convert string to float: ' '` at `float(row['amount'])`
scenarios.explain: Boundary bug. Empty/whitespace amount in the CSV. Fix: validate at read with a stricter parser; coerce '' → 0 only if your business rule allows it, otherwise raise.

scenarios.situation: `KeyError: 'name'` at `row['name']`. The CSV header is `'name '` (trailing space).
scenarios.explain: Boundary bug, the silent kind. Excel exports often add stray whitespace. Fix: normalize headers — `reader.fieldnames = [n.strip() for n in reader.fieldnames]` before iterating.

scenarios.situation: `ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero` at `total / count` where count was loaded from the file.
scenarios.explain: Middle-logic bug. The pipeline allowed an empty group through. Fix: guard with `if count == 0: continue` or raise an explicit error if zero is unexpected.

Environment bug. Either pandas isn't installed in the venv that's running this script, or the script isn't being run with the right interpreter. Fix: `pip install pandas` in the active venv. Long-term fix: a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml.

scenarios.situation: `json.JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)` when reading the file you just wrote.
scenarios.explain: Boundary bug. The write half of your pipeline produced an empty or truncated file (often: the program crashed mid-write, or you opened in 'w' but wrote no data). Fix: write atomically — to a tmp file, then rename.

scenarios.situation: `UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 14`
scenarios.explain: Boundary bug. The file is not UTF-8 (probably latin-1 or windows-1252 from an Indian-accountant Excel export). Fix: detect with `chardet` or specify the right encoding explicitly. Don't 'errors=ignore' it; you'll silently lose the ₹ sign.

blocks.title: The classic trap: 'errors=ignore' as a fix
blocks.md:
When you hit a UnicodeDecodeError, the lazy fix is `open(path, encoding='utf-8', errors='ignore')`. **Don't.** This silently drops bytes. The ₹ sign disappears. The 'café' becomes 'caf'. You don't know what you've lost.

Fix it properly: figure out the actual encoding (`file -i path`, or use `chardet`), and decode correctly. Bad data found at the boundary should *fail*, not be silently mutilated. Future-you will thank present-you for the loud failure.

blocks.prompt: You ship the pipeline. A user reports it crashes on their CSV. Where do you look FIRST?

choices.label: The first line of the traceback (the call site in your code) and the data in the offending row
